# Why this note exists {.unnumbered}

The definition of a sigma-field is compact, but proofs involving sigma-fields
can feel unmanageably large. A probability measure on the real line is defined
on every Borel set, yet statisticians usually specify or compare it using a
much smaller collection, such as intervals or half-lines.

This note develops the tools that justify that move. Its central principle is

> Start with a small class of sets that generates the events of interest, then
> use a closure theorem to extend a statement from the small class to the full
> sigma-field.

This is general measure-theory knowledge for statistics. It is **not required
for a first reading of Walker's chapter**. Return to it when a proof says that
two probability laws agree on a generating class, constructs a product law,
or invokes the pi-lambda theorem.

## What this note assumes

Read
[Sets, functions, inverse images, and pushforwards](sets-functions-and-pushforwards.qmd)
and the definitions of sigma-fields and measures in
[Measure and probability foundations](measure-probability-foundations.qmd#sigma-field-definition).
No real-analysis or proof-based probability course is assumed.

# Generated sigma-fields {#generated-sigma-fields}

Let $\mathcal C$ be any collection of subsets of a set $\Omega$. The
**sigma-field generated by $\mathcal C$**, written

$$
\sigma(\mathcal C),
$$

is the smallest sigma-field containing every set in $\mathcal C$.

"Smallest" has a precise set-inclusion meaning. If $\mathcal F$ is any
sigma-field with $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal F$, then

$$
\sigma(\mathcal C)\subseteq\mathcal F.
$$

Equivalently, $\sigma(\mathcal C)$ is the intersection of all sigma-fields
that contain $\mathcal C$. An intersection of sigma-fields is again a
sigma-field, so this definition produces a unique object.

The generator $\mathcal C$ does not itself need to be a sigma-field. Its role
is to name the basic sets; $\sigma(\mathcal C)$ adds every complement,
countable union, and countable intersection forced by the sigma-field rules.

## A finite example {#generated-finite-example}

Let

$$
\Omega=\{1,2,3,4\},
\qquad
\mathcal C=\bigl\{\{1,2\}\bigr\}.
$$

Any sigma-field containing $\{1,2\}$ must also contain its complement
$\{3,4\}$, along with $\emptyset$ and $\Omega$. These four sets already form a
sigma-field, so

$$
\sigma(\mathcal C)
=\{\emptyset,\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\Omega\}.
$$

This sigma-field can distinguish whether the outcome lies in the first pair
or the second pair, but it cannot distinguish 1 from 2.

# Borel sigma-fields {#borel-sigma-fields}

The **Borel sigma-field** on the real line is

$$
\mathcal B(\mathbb R)=\sigma\{(a,b):a<b\}.
$$

It is generated by the open intervals. The same sigma-field is generated by
many other convenient classes, including

$$
\{(-\infty,t]:t\in\mathbb R\}
\quad\text{or}\quad
\{(a,b]:a<b\}.
$$

These equivalences matter statistically. A cumulative distribution function
reports probabilities of the half-lines $(-\infty,t]$. Because those
half-lines generate $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, the CDF contains enough
information to determine the probability measure on every Borel event.

The statement does not mean that every Borel set is one half-line. It means
that the sigma-field closure operations generate all Borel sets from the
half-lines.

# Why a smaller proof class is useful {#why-proof-classes}

Suppose $P$ and $Q$ are probability measures on
$(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. Directly checking

$$
P(A)=Q(A)
\quad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal F
$$

may be impossible because $\mathcal F$ is enormous. It would be helpful to
verify equality on a manageable generator $\mathcal C$ and then extend it.

A generator by itself is not always enough for the extension argument. The
pi-lambda method pairs two set classes whose closure properties fit probability
measures particularly well.

# Pi-systems {#pi-systems}

A collection $\mathcal P$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is a **pi-system** if it is
closed under finite intersections:

$$
A,B\in\mathcal P
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
A\cap B\in\mathcal P.
$$

The name uses the Greek letter pi because intersection resembles a finite
product of event indicators. A pi-system need not contain complements or
unions and therefore need not be a sigma-field.

Examples include

- half-lines $(-\infty,t]$ on $\mathbb R$;
- rectangles $A\times B$ in a product space;
- cylinder events depending on finitely many coordinates of a sequence.

For half-lines,

$$
(-\infty,s]\cap(-\infty,t]
=(-\infty,\min\{s,t\}],
$$

so the class is closed under intersection.

# Dynkin or lambda systems {#dynkin-systems}

A collection $\mathcal L$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is a **Dynkin system**, also
called a **lambda system**, if

1. $\Omega\in\mathcal L$;
2. $A,B\in\mathcal L$ and $A\subseteq B$ imply $B\setminus A\in\mathcal L$;
3. for pairwise disjoint $A_1,A_2,\ldots\in\mathcal L$,
   $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\in\mathcal L$.

An equivalent definition uses closure under complements and under countable
unions of pairwise disjoint sets.

Every sigma-field is a Dynkin system. A Dynkin system can be smaller because
it need not be closed under intersections or arbitrary countable unions.

The Dynkin-system rules mirror properties that are easy to preserve under a
probability measure. For example, if $P(A)=Q(A)$ and $A\subseteq B$ with
$P(B)=Q(B)$, then

$$
P(B\setminus A)=P(B)-P(A)=Q(B)-Q(A)=Q(B\setminus A).
$$

Countable additivity similarly preserves equality across disjoint unions.

# The pi-lambda theorem {#pi-lambda-theorem}

The **pi-lambda theorem** states:

> If $\mathcal P$ is a pi-system, then the smallest Dynkin system containing
> $\mathcal P$ equals the sigma-field generated by $\mathcal P$.

Writing $\lambda(\mathcal P)$ for that smallest Dynkin system,

$$
\lambda(\mathcal P)=\sigma(\mathcal P).
$$

The theorem supplies a reusable proof pattern:

1. choose a pi-system $\mathcal P$ that generates the desired sigma-field;
2. let $\mathcal L$ be the sets on which the desired statement is true;
3. prove that $\mathcal L$ is a Dynkin system;
4. verify that $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal L$;
5. conclude that
   $\sigma(\mathcal P)=\lambda(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal L$.

The theorem's proof is optional at this stage. The key skill is recognizing
when a setwise statistical claim forms a Dynkin system.

# Statistical use 1: a CDF determines a law {#cdf-determines-law}

Let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on
$(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ and suppose

$$
P\{(-\infty,t]\}=Q\{(-\infty,t]\}
\quad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.
$$

The half-lines form a pi-system and generate $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. Define

$$
\mathcal L=\{A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R):P(A)=Q(A)\}.
$$

Because $P$ and $Q$ are probability measures, $\mathcal L$ is a Dynkin
system. It contains every generating half-line. The pi-lambda theorem therefore
gives

$$
P(A)=Q(A)
\quad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).
$$

Thus equal CDFs imply equal probability distributions, not merely equal
probabilities for a special collection of intervals.

# Statistical use 2: identifying joint laws {#identifying-joint-laws}

On $\mathbb R^d$, lower-left rectangles

$$
(-\infty,t_1]\times\cdots\times(-\infty,t_d]
$$

form a pi-system that generates $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$. Agreement of two
probability measures on all such rectangles therefore implies agreement on
all Borel events. This is why a multivariate CDF determines a joint law.

More generally, probability models on product spaces are often specified
first on rectangles. The extension machinery creates a measure on the
generated product sigma-field, and the pi-lambda theorem proves uniqueness.

# Statistical use 3: proving independence {#proving-independence}

Two sigma-fields $\mathcal F_1$ and $\mathcal F_2$ are independent if

$$
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)
\quad
\text{for every }A\in\mathcal F_1,
\ B\in\mathcal F_2.
$$

If $\mathcal P_1$ and $\mathcal P_2$ are pi-systems generating
$\mathcal F_1$ and $\mathcal F_2$, it is enough to verify the factorization on
$A\in\mathcal P_1$ and $B\in\mathcal P_2$. Applying the pi-lambda theorem in
one coordinate and then the other extends the identity to the full
sigma-fields.

This is why independence proofs commonly begin with intervals, rectangles, or
cylinder events rather than arbitrary measurable sets.

# How this fits with measure construction {#relation-to-extension}

The pi-lambda theorem primarily proves **uniqueness** and extends identities
for measures that already exist. A different question is how to construct a
measure from proposed values on a small set class.

That construction uses algebras, premeasures, outer measures, and the
Caratheodory extension theorem. It is developed in
[Premeasures and measure extension](premeasures-and-measure-extension.qmd).

| Goal | Main tool |
|---|---|
| Extend an equality or independence statement | Pi-lambda theorem |
| Construct a measure from interval or rectangle values | Caratheodory extension |
| Show the resulting measure is unique | Extension theorem and/or pi-lambda method |

# Check your understanding

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. If $\mathcal C$ generates $\mathcal F$, must $\mathcal C$ itself be a
sigma-field?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

No. A generator can be much smaller. It only needs to be a collection whose
sigma-field closure is $\mathcal F$. For example, the half-lines
$(-\infty,t]$ are not closed under complements, but they generate
$\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$.
:::

**2. Why do the half-lines $(-\infty,t]$ form a pi-system?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The intersection of any two remains in the class:

$$
(-\infty,s]\cap(-\infty,t]
=(-\infty,\min\{s,t\}].
$$

Closure under finite intersections is exactly the pi-system requirement.
:::

**3. What extra closure property does a sigma-field have that a Dynkin system
need not have?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

A sigma-field is closed under arbitrary countable unions and hence finite
intersections. A Dynkin system is only required to be closed under complements
and countable **disjoint** unions. A class that is both a pi-system and a
Dynkin system is a sigma-field.
:::

**4. Two probability measures agree on every half-line $(-\infty,t]$. What
allows us to conclude that they agree on every Borel set?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The half-lines form a pi-system generating $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. The sets
on which the two probability measures agree form a Dynkin system. The
pi-lambda theorem extends agreement from the generating pi-system to the whole
Borel sigma-field.
:::

**5. Is the pi-lambda theorem mainly an existence theorem or an extension and
uniqueness tool?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

It is mainly an extension and uniqueness tool. It propagates a setwise
statement from a generating pi-system to the generated sigma-field. Constructing
a new measure from proposed values usually requires a premeasure and the
Caratheodory extension theorem.
:::

**6. Why are rectangles useful in joint-distribution arguments?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Rectangles are easy to evaluate, are closed under finite intersections, and
generate the product sigma-field. Equality or factorization verified on
rectangles can therefore be extended to all measurable events using the
pi-lambda method.
:::
